title: Quantifying the sensitivity of ephemeral streams to land disturbance activities in arid ecosystems at the watershed scale
abstract: Large areas of public lands administered by the Bureau of Land Management and located in arid regions of the southwestern United States are being considered for the development of utility-scale solar energy facilities. Land-disturbing activities in these desert, alluvium-filled valleys have the potential to adversely affect the hydrologic and ecologic functions of ephemeral streams. Regulation and management of ephemeral streams typically falls under a spectrum of federal, state, and local programs, but scientifically based guidelines for protecting ephemeral streams with respect to land-development activities are largely nonexistent. This study developed an assessment approach for quantifying the sensitivity to land disturbance of ephemeral stream reaches located in proposed solar energy zones (SEZs). The ephemeral stream assessment approach used publicly-available geospatial data on hydrology, topography, surficial geology, and soil characteristics, as well as high-resolution aerial imagery. These datasets were used to inform a professional judgment-based score index of potential land disturbance impacts on selected critical functions of ephemeral streams, including flow and sediment conveyance, ecological habitat value, and groundwater recharge. The total sensitivity scores (sum of scores for the critical stream functions of flow and sediment conveyance, ecological habitats, and groundwater recharge) were used to identify highly sensitive stream reaches to inform decisions on developable areas in SEZs. Total sensitivity scores typically reflected the scores of the individual stream functions; some exceptions pertain to groundwater recharge and ecological habitats. The primary limitations of this assessment approach were the lack of high-resolution identification of ephemeral stream channels in the existing National Hydrography Dataset, and the lack of mechanistic processes describing potential impacts on ephemeral stream functions at the watershed scale. The primary strength of this assessment approach is that it allows watershed-scale planning for low-impact development in arid ecosystems; the qualitative scoring of potential impacts can also be adjusted to accommodate new geospatial data, and to allow for expert and stakeholder input into decisions regarding the identification and potential avoidance of highly sensitive stream reaches.

# **Quantifying the sensitivity of ephemeral streams to land disturbance activities in arid ecosystems at the watershed scale**

**Ben L. O’Connor · Yuki Hamada · Esther E. Bowen · Mark A. Grippo · Heidi M. Hartmann · Terri L. Patton · Robert A. Van Lonkhuyzen · Adrianne E. Carr**

Received: 20 November 2013 / Accepted: 30 June 2014 / Published online: 17 August 2014 © Springer International Publishing Switzerland 2014

in proposed solar energy zones (SEZs). The ephemeral stream assessment approach used publicly-available geospatial data on hydrology, topography, surficial geology, and soil characteristics, as well as highresolution aerial imagery. These datasets were used to inform a professional judgment-based score index of potential land disturbance impacts on selected critical functions of ephemeral streams, including flow and sediment conveyance, ecological habitat value, and groundwater recharge. The primary strength of this assessment approach is that it allows watershed-scale planning for low-impact development in arid ecosystems; the qualitative scoring of potential impacts can also be adjusted to accommodate new geospatial data, and to allow for expert and stakeholder input into decisions regarding the identification and potential avoidance of highly sensitive stream reaches.

**Keywords** Ephemeral streams · Land disturbance · Arid ecosystems · Watershed characteristics · Environmental assessment

## **Introduction**

Ephemeral streams (including intermittent and temporary streams) are dry for some portion of the year and convey water in response to hydrologic events that are seasonal or episodic in nature such as snowmelt runoff, surface water-groundwater interactions, and flash floods. In humid regions, ephemeral streams are predominantly headwater channels, but in arid regions, they account for the majority of stream channel length throughout a watershed (Caruso and Haynes 2011). This study focuses on watersheds in arid regions where the physical characteristics of ephemeral streams vary with respect to climatic drivers of episodic rainfall inputs (Pool 2005), and with respect to watershed characteristics such as elevation, slope, surficial soils, and parent geologic materials (Wohl et al. 2007; Levick et al. 2008). Ephemeral streams are often associated with piedmont (e.g., alluvial fans) and valley regions in arid watersheds, and have morphologies consisting of both single- and multithreaded channels, having compound cross-sections, and forming both anabranching and distributary channel network patterns (Tooth 2000; Nanson et al. 2002; Field and Lichvar 2007).

Several key hydrologic and ecologic functions are associated with ephemeral streams; they include water and sediment transport, surface and subsurface water storage, groundwater recharge, nutrient and organic material transport, and the establishment of a variety of habitat conditions and biologic migration corridors (Levick et al. 2008). Ephemeral streams have a unique biodiversity signature resulting from communities developing under extreme conditions, spanning from episodic flood disturbances to long periods of drying (Steward et al. 2012). Riparian biotic communities are established across gradients of water availability tolerances resulting in a close coupling between the ecological and hydrologic conditions of ephemeral stream channel networks (Shaw and Cooper 2008). Landscape disturbances (both natural and anthropogenic) affect the connectivity and functioning of ephemeral stream networks and thereby alter the delivery of water, nutrients, sediments, and

biota throughout the watershed. Changes in hydrologic processes caused by landscape disturbances ultimately result in a loss in biodiversity from which it can take a long time to recover due to infrequent and episodic inputs of water in arid regions (Levick et al. 2008).

Anthropogenic disturbances to ephemeral streams in arid regions are primarily associated with agriculture, grazing, urbanization, and energy development (Field and Lichvar 2007). In general, these types of landscape disturbances involve surface grading, vegetation removal, soil compaction, and groundwater withdrawals that have both direct and indirect impacts due to the inherent linkages among riparian vegetation, soil characteristics, surface water-groundwater interactions, and channel morphology in arid ecosystems (Levick et al. 2008; Shaw and Cooper 2008). In addition to these landscape disturbances, ephemeral stream channels are often removed by surface grading, which causes surface flows to be routed through large-capacity channels (both preexisting and modified channels) and stormwater infrastructure, resulting in increased erosion rates and a more rapid flow of water through a watershed (Chin and Gregory 2001; Field and Lichvar 2007; Duniway and Herrick 2011). One of the more striking examples of impacts on ephemeral stream channel networks can be seen at the historic location of Camp Ironside in the Mojave Desert of California, where 2 years of extensive land disturbance for military training occurred during World War II and the system still does not yet show signs of recovery (Nichols and Bierman 2001).

Hydrologic and fluvial processes in arid systems are not as well understood as their counterparts in humid regions and, in particular, streams in arid regions typically do not tend toward an equilibrium state (i.e., predictable channel adjustments relative to hydrologic inputs) (Tooth 2000). Steward et al. (2012) describe several knowledge gaps that exist pertaining to ecological processes of ephemeral streams; these gaps include research questions regarding the role of ephemeral streams in providing biodiversity, critical habitat, and terrestrial biologic corridors, as well as mediating biogeochemical processes such as carbon and nutrient cycling. Hydrologic and ecologic functions of ephemeral streams have been studied in a variety of settings including experimental watersheds such as Walnut Gulch, Arizona, which focused on integrative ecosystem functionality (Moran et al. 2008).

However, studies examining landscape disturbances of ephemeral stream channel networks are more piecemeal in nature, often involving isolated land disturbances, or focusing on a particular hydrologic or ecologic function of interest such that watershedscale assessments of anticipated impacts on ephemeral streams from land disturbances are largely nonexistent (Leu et al. 2008; Turnbull et al. 2008; Duniway and Herrick 2011; Brady et al. 2013).

Not only are arid watersheds susceptible to landscape disturbances, ephemeral streams typically receive fewer environmental protections in comparison to perennial streams, partially because of landowner perceptions regarding what is, and what is not, considered a stream (Armstrong et al. 2012). In the United States, the Clean Water Act (CWA) is a key mechanism for protecting aquatic resources. However, ephemeral streams are not considered to be jurisdictional waters of the United States, and thus are not covered by the CWA, unless a significant nexus to navigable waters is established (EPA 2008). Several studies have demonstrated the hydrologic and ecologic connectivity of streams from headwaters to downstream reaches, which suggests the need for a more science-based and universal definition of jurisdictional waters under the CWA (e.g., Nadeau and Rains 2007; Caruso and Haynes2011). Historically, jurisdictional water determinations have primarily been made on a case-by-case basis by local offices of the US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) and the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA); this often results in inconsistencies from region to region among the jurisdictional water determinations that affect ephemeral streams (Caruso 2011). In order to increase the transparency and consistency of jurisdictional water determinations, the USACE and EPA have developed a proposed rule that more extensively defines the scope of waters protected under the CWA. This proposed ruling was developed based on an extensive review of scientific literature examining the connectivity of physical, chemical, and biological characteristics throughout a watershed (USACE and EPA 2014). The proposed rule is currently in its public comment period (EPA 2014).

State regulations, such as California’s Lake and Streambed Alteration Program (CDFW 2013) can be more universal in applying stream permitting programs to all stream channels regardless of whether they are perennial, intermittent, or ephemeral in

nature. However, knowledge gaps regarding the impacts of land disturbance to the coupled hydrologic and ecologic functions of ephemeral stream networks often result in developers submitting inappropriate project designs and ineffective mitigation measures, which can result in permitting delays (Brady et al. 2013). In addition, permitting programs are applied on a case-by-case basis, so it is difficult to assess the potential impacts at the watershed scale. The current federal and state regulatory framework is designed such that when a landscape disturbance is proposed, it is followed by an evaluation of impacts on water bodies that results in regulators requesting alterations to the planned disturbance or specifying certain mitigation measures. This framework makes it difficult for managers to plan for development and land use changes (such as roads, mining, and energy development) in a manner that minimizes ecosystem impacts associated with alterations to ephemeral streams at the watershed scale.

Land managers need assessment tools for evaluating potential impacts on the hydrologic and ecologic functioning of ephemeral stream channel networks, given their ubiquitous nature and the expansion of land disturbance activities in arid regions (Wohl et al. 2007; Leu et al. 2008; Turnbull et al. 2008). Assessment procedures exist for classifying streams by their physical structure and indices of biological compositions in humid regions (Karr 1991; Poff 1996; Kaufmann et al. 1999). However, counterpart assessment procedures for arid systems have primarily focused on hazards from alluvial fan flooding and debris flows (House 2005; Robins et al. 2009). Given the lack of assessment approaches that integrate hydrologic and ecologic functions at the watershed scale for arid regions, decisions regarding potential land disturbances can use risk assessment approaches that incorporate existing knowledge and datasets pertaining to the physical and biologic characteristics of the watershed such as weight-of-evidence or multiple-attribute analyses (Finnveden et al. 2003; Suter and Cormier 2011). These types of risk assessment approaches use some combination of quantitative and qualitative data to inform professional judgment in making decisions regarding the process of interest. The use of professional judgment for an environmental assessment approach introduces value judgments by the assessors, which need to be considered when evaluating the results of the assessment (Weed 2005). However,

these types of value judgments can be useful because many of the stream assessment protocols outlined in the CWA include a “value” factor that provides the opportunity to prioritize compensatory mitigation measures based on the professional judgment of the regulatory agencies (Somerville and Pruitt 2004). The incorporation of professional judgment to an assessment approach also has the potential to engage stakeholder groups in evaluating potential land disturbance alternatives.

In 2012, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) initiated its solar energy program, which in part identified solar energy zones (SEZs) that cover over 1,150 km[2] of public lands in the southwestern US, where the BLM plans to prioritize development of utility-scale solar facilities (BLM 2012b). The development of the BLM’s solar energy program involved interactions with cooperating agencies, regulators, environmental groups, solar energy developers, and the general public, which collectively identified several concerns regarding impacts on ephemeral streams that ranged from flooding issues to loss of critical habitat, as well as developers’ concerns regarding feasibility of avoiding impacts on ephemeral streams, given their ubiquitous presence in arid environments (BLM 2012b). Predicting impacts associated with proposed solar energy development is difficult because there is a lack of understanding about all the potential impacts on coupled hydrologic and ecological processes (Duniway and Herrick 2011), and existing guidelines for low-impact development associated with ephemeral streams in arid regions primarily relate to flood risks on alluvial fans (NRC 1996; Alluvial Fan Task Force 2010). For this study, a weight of evidence approach was developed that uses available data sources to inform professional judgment in developing a scoring index that rates individual stream reaches with respect to their sensitivity to landscape disturbance.

This study was motivated by the need to have a planning-level tool to assess the functionality of ephemeral streams at a watershed scale in order to consider the environmental impacts associated with utility-scale solar energy development, as well as to guide decisions on identifying avoidance and potential mitigation areas. The ephemeral stream assessment approach used publicly-available geospatial, soil, and hydrologic data on topography, surficial geology, historical peak discharges, and soil characteristics, as

well as high-resolution aerial imagery. These datasets were used to inform a professional judgment-based score index of potential land disturbance impacts on flow and sediment conveyance, ecological habitats, and groundwater recharge. A slope-based algorithm was developed to identify valley, piedmont, and mountain areas within the study regions, and the sensitivity to disturbance index was stratified among these regions to account for the dynamics in ephemeral stream functions that can vary from upland to lowland regions of a watershed. The sensitivity to disturbance metric was applied to mapped ephemeral stream channels in the study regions for SEZs that were evaluated in the BLM’s _Programmatic Environmental Impact Statement for Solar Energy Development in Six Southwestern States_ (solar PEIS). The appropriateness and limitations of this planning-level tool for ephemeral streams were assessed with respect to the expert-based scoring criteria for the critical functions of ephemeral streams, as well as with respect to the type and resolution of available datasets used to map landscape features and ephemeral stream channel networks.

## **Study area**

The BLM’s solar energy program focuses on public lands in the southwest US, and 17 SEZs were evaluated in its Solar PEIS (BLM 2012b). Two additional SEZs have been identified since the release of the solar PEIS, and a framework has been developed to identify others in the future, but this study focuses on the 17 SEZs analyzed in the Solar PEIS. The 17 SEZs were established as priority areas for utilityscale solar energy development through the BLM’s record of decision issued in October 2012 (BLM 2012a). The areas selected for SEZs were originally identified by BLM field offices using the general criteria of lands with slopes less than 5 %, solar insolation levels greater than 6.5 kWh/m[2] /day, and minimal resource conflicts (environmental, recreation, or other industrial land uses) (BLM 2012b). Through the environmental assessment associated with the solar PEIS, the original 24 proposed SEZs were reduced to the 17 described in the final Solar PEIS. The 17 SEZs are primarily located within the basin and range physiographic province with the exception of the four SEZs located in Colorado that are a part of the Southern Rocky Mountains physiographic province (Fig. 1).

**Fig. 1** Locations of analysis watersheds along with physiographic province boundaries

The SEZs range in size between 4 and 599 km[2] , with average elevations ranging from 29 to 2,395 m above mean sea level (Table 1).

The assessment of ephemeral streams for each SEZ was performed within a region made up of anywhere from one to eight US Geological Survey (USGS) watersheds that were intersected by the SEZ boundaries (watersheds at the Hydrologic Unit Code—HUC10 level were used). This resulted in ephemeral stream analysis watersheds that covered between 555 and 4,205 km[2] with total stream channel lengths ranging from 21 to 8,314 km according to the high-resolution (1:24,000) National Hydrography Dataset (NHD) (Table 2). The land cover characteristics of the SEZs and the analysis watersheds are typical of arid and semiarid basin valleys, and Table 3 lists their primary land uses, soil types, and vegetation classifications. Most of the SEZs are located on undeveloped lands within desert basins that also

have agricultural and industrial land uses within their watersheds. Soils are predominantly loams of various textures, with some playa and sand dune features in certain SEZs. Vegetation is sparse to moderately dense in the SEZs with typical desert and intermountain shrublands, which include creosotebush, sagebrush, saltbush-greasewood, and palo verde-cactus (BLM 2012b). Further information regarding environmental analyses relevant to the SEZs can be found on the BLM’s Solar Energy Program website (http://blmsolar.anl.gov).

The ephemeral stream functions were evaluated with respect to landscape characteristics to account for how hydrologic and ecologic processes vary with respect to physical conditions and location within a watershed (Shaw and Cooper 2008). ## Topographic setting

The topographic conditions of the basin and range physiographic province consist of narrow mountain ranges with arid and semiarid valleys in between (Graf 1987). From this generalized conceptual model of topography, stream reaches were defined as being within mountain, piedmont, or valley regions. Distributions of the pixel densities (the number of pixels in each binned-slope class divided by the total number of pixels in the study region) for the 100 slope classes revealed a similar pattern among all the SEZs; these distributions were used to distinguish valley, piedmont, and mountain areas for each SEZ study region (Fig. 2a). The distributions of pixel density were characterized as having small peaks associated

with slope classes 1 and 99, along with a large peak that occurred between slope classes 5 and 30. ## Surficial geology and soil-hydrologic characteristics

Surficial geology maps were obtained from the National Geologic Map Database (USGS 2012a), and a total of 12 surficial geology units were identified for all SEZ study regions (Table 4). The Soil Survey Geographic (SSURGO) database (NRCS 2012) was used

to specify four metrics that quantify soil-hydrologic characteristics relevant to ephemeral streams. The four soil-hydrologic metrics include flooding frequency, available water storage in the top 150 cm of soil, hydrologic group, and hydric class. The flooding frequency is the annual highest probability of a flood event expressed as a class of either none, very rare, rare, occasional, frequent, or very frequent. The available water storage is the amount of water (expressed as centimeters of water) stored by the top 150 cm of soil after drainage. The hydrologic group categorizes runoff potential among soil conditions into four groups (A, B, C, and D) that range from group A, which has low runoff potential and high infiltration potential, to group D, which has high runoff potential and low infiltration potential. The hydric class is a measure of the soil moisture conditions that support hydrophytic vegetation and can be classified as all hydric, partially hydric, or not hydric.

## Scoring index for stream sensitivity

An index was developed using professional judgment that rated the potential for land disturbance to affect the critical functions of ephemeral streams, including flow and sediment conveyance, ecological habitat value, and groundwater recharge. The index ranged from 1 (low sensitivity to disturbance) to 5 (high sensitivity to disturbance) and rated the sensitivity to disturbance of the three critical functions of ephemeral streams according to six landscape characteristics describing the topographic setting (piedmont or valley region), surficial geology (surficial geologic units), and soil hydrologic characteristics (flood frequency, available water storage, hydrologic group, and hydric class). Resource specialists including two hydrologists, two ecologists, and two geologists were provided information about the six landscape characteristics. They were asked to assign a score for each potential value of the landscape characteristics with respect to how each characteristic’s condition would relate to its potential sensitivity to disturbance for each of the three critical functions. For example, topographic setting had two potential values (piedmont or valley), and resource specialists assigned scores that reflected their views on the sensitivity to disturbance with respect to each of the three critical functions that could occur in piedmont and valley regions separately.

The mean index scores among resource specialists were applied in the ephemeral stream sensitivity analyses, which are shown in Table 4.

Ephemeral stream channel segments within SEZs were identified using NHD data, which depicts streams as a set of flow lines derived from digital line graphs (DLGs) based on topographic maps (at a minimum resolution of 1:24,000) (USGS 2012b). Individual flow lines of ephemeral stream channels were intersected with six landscape characteristic layers possessing score values for each of the three critical functions. Landscape characteristic layers included topographic setting, surficial geology, and four metrics of soil-hydrologic characteristics (Fig. 3). The total sensitivity to disturbance was the sum of index scores for each of the three integral

functions. For the solar PEIS, stream reaches were further characterized as having a high, moderate, or low sensitivity to disturbance based on the value of the total score; these groupings were set using the mean and standard deviation of the total scores over all stream reaches analyzed (BLM 2012b). This study focuses on sensitivity to disturbance index scores by themselves.

Ephemeral stream reaches that crossed previously disturbed areas (e.g., developed areas and agricultural fields that were identified using aerial imagery) were excluded from the sensitivity to disturbance analysis. This was done to avoid a false-positive

In addition, ephemeral stream reaches associated with upland regions of the watershed (defined by surface elevations greater than the median elevation in the analysis watershed) were excluded from the analysis because siting criteria described in the Solar PEIS would limit land disturbance activities to the lowland regions (BLM 2012b). For this purpose, the median elevation of the watershed was used as a threshold between the upland and lowland portions of the watershed, and the sensitivity to disturbance was only applied to stream reaches in the lowland portion of the study watershed.

## **Results**

## Topographic setting

The topographic setting (mountain, piedmont, or valley) analysis for each study watershed depicted similar patterns in the distribution of slope classes. The SEZs located in Colorado within the Southern Rocky Mountains physiographic province exhibited major differences in slope class distribution in comparison with all the other SEZs within the basin and range physiographic province (Fig. 4). With respect to slope classes, SEZs were largely clustered in similar geographical regions of each state, and SEZs within individual states had nearly identical histogram patterns for slope classes. In the basin and range physiographic province, the large peak in the slope class histogram associated with the valley bottom varied between slope classes 5 and 30, and the width of the large peak is a general indication of the transition from valley to mountain regions or the broadness of the piedmont region (Fig. 4a). The Colorado SEZs within the Southern Rocky Mountains physiographic province had a slightly different pattern in the histogram of slope classes; the valley peak was more of a plateau from slope classes 1 to 10 (Fig. 4b). This pattern of a broad range in slope classes indicates that there was more topographic variation on the valley floor for these Colorado watersheds than for the other SEZ watersheds in the basin and range physiographic province.

**Fig. 4** Distribution of pixel density among slope classes for study watersheds in states **a** within the Basin and Range physiographic province, and **b** within the Southern Rocky Mountains physiographic province

## Scoring index and sensitivity to disturbance

The sensitivity to disturbance index scores (Table 4) show the average score and the range of scores tallied from all the resource specialists. Averaging the index scores resulted in no scores of 5, and summing the minimum and maximum potential scores for each of the three stream functions resulted in a

range of possible scores from 12 to 22 for flow and sediment conveyance, 14 to 24 for ecological habitats, and 8 to 23 for groundwater recharge. The total index score was the sum of scores for all three stream functions and had a potential range from 34 to 69. The index score values for the six landscape characteristics among the three stream functions suggested that stream reaches with high sensitivity to disturbance were likely in piedmont regions; had a surface geology of alluvial, playa, sand dune, or lacustrine sediments; and had soil-hydrologic characteristics of high infiltration rates that experienced relatively frequent flooding. The variability in index score values for individual landscape characteristics among the three stream functions was typically small (less than 2), with the exception of topographic setting and soil hydrologic group with respect to flow and sediment conveyance, and in soil flood frequency with respect to ecological habitat scores.

The SEZs and their associated study watersheds varied greatly in area, but in general SEZs covered 1 to 9 % of their watershed, with the exception of the Riverside East SEZ, which covered approximately 15 % of its watershed (Tables 1 and 2). The study watersheds typically contained between 1 and 2.4 km of stream channel length per square kilometer (channel density) (Table 2), with the exception of the Imperial East SEZ watershed, which was almost devoid of stream channels. Channel densities were typically low within the SEZs themselves, with channel densities less than 1 km/km[2] for 7 of the 17 SEZs (Brenda, Imperial East, Millers, Afton, Escalante Valley, Milford Flats South, and Fourmile East); however, the Gillespie and Amargosa Valley SEZs had high channel densities of 4.4 and 2.1 km/km[2] , respectively (Table 1). The percentage of stream channels assessed in each of the study watersheds ranged between 38 and 87 % of the total channel length (mountain region reaches and previously disturbed reaches were excluded from the analysis), although the percentage of stream length assessed was lower for the watersheds in the Southern Rocky Mountains physiographic province (Table 2). These watersheds in the Southern Rocky Mountains province had several stream reaches located in upland regions (i.e., surface elevations greater than median elevation of the watershed), as well as stream reaches associated with agricultural fields within the San Luis Valley of southern Colorado.

The distribution of the total index scores over the 17 study watersheds (measured by the total stream length associated with each score value) depicted a discrete pattern with a general central tendency (Fig. 5). The majority of stream channel lengths within the study watersheds had total index scores that ranged between 46 and 57, and individual stream function scores ranged between 15 and 20 (Fig. 5a, b, respectively). The distribution of stream function scores suggested that flow and sediment conveyance had the narrowest range in scores, while groundwater recharge had the broadest range in scores (Fig. 5b). For individual

SEZ watersheds, the distribution of total index scores varied, but it exhibited similar patterns for SEZs in similar regional settings. The cumulative distribution function of the total stream length associated with individual total index score values (cumulative from low to high total index score) was used to compare the distribution of total index scores among SEZ watersheds. The Amargosa Valley SEZ watershed had the highest overall total index scores (i.e., the cumulative distribution function was the furthest to the right) of the 17 study watersheds assessed (Fig. 6a), while the Brenda SEZ watershed had the lowest overall

total index scores (data not shown). The five SEZ watersheds in Nevada demonstrated a similarly broad range in total index scores, which is shown by the relatively shallow slope of the cumulative distribution functions (Fig. 6a), while the four SEZ watersheds in Colorado had a narrow range in score values depicted by the relatively steep slope over a narrow range in total index scores (Fig. 6b). In addition, for three SEZ watersheds in Nevada (Amargosa Valley, Gold Point, and Millers), between 10 and 20 % of their stream lengths had a total index score greater than 57, the largest total index score for all the the Colorado SEZ watersheds (Fig. 6a, b).

The spatial distribution of the sensitivity to disturbance index throughout the study watersheds was used to inform decisions regarding nondevelopment and potential mitigation regions as a part of the solar PEIS, which includes maps for all 17 study watersheds (BLM 2012b). For the Amargosa Valley SEZ watershed, the braided stream channels of the Amargosa River, which flows from north to south across the watershed, had high total index scores along the southwestern edge of the SEZ; this portion of the SEZ was designated as a nondevelopment area in the Solar PEIS (Fig. 7a). The scores for the individual stream functions of flow and sediment conveyance, ecological habitat value, and groundwater recharge all showed similar patterns with respect to the spatial distribution of stream function index scores (Fig. 7a–c). However, there were some instances where the total index score was not representative of the scores for one of the individual stream functions. Specifically, the ecological habitat scores for the Fourmile East SEZ watershed and the groundwater recharge scores for the Riverside East, Escalante Valley, and De Tilla Gulch SEZ watersheds were not fully reflected by their total index scores (BLM 2012b). For example, examining the difference between the total index scores and the index scores for groundwater recharge for the De Tilla Gulch SEZ watershed shows that several stream reaches draining the San Juan Mountains (to the north of the SEZ) are critical for groundwater recharge but were only scored as having a moderate sensitivity to disturbance because of the lower scores associated with flow and sediment conveyance, as well as ecological habitats (Fig. 8).

## **Discussion**

This study developed an approach for assessing potential impacts on ephemeral streams resulting from land disturbance associated with utility-scale solar energy development. The conceptual model for this assessment approach examined the critical ecosystem functions of flow and sediment conveyance, ecological habitat value, and groundwater recharge. These hydrologic and ecologic functions were assumed to be geographically distinct in valley, piedmont, and mountain regions of the watershed, as well as with respect to surficial geology and habitat characteristics.

These landscape characteristics were used to stratify a professional judgment-based score index pertaining to the degree of sensitivity to land disturbance for individual ephemeral stream reaches in the analysis watersheds. This conceptual model of landscape controls on the hydrologic and ecologic functioning of streams is analogous to stream classification and condition assessments used for streams in humid regions (Poff 1996; Kaufmann et al. 1999). The choice of the specific hydrologic and ecologic functions to assess was driven by stakeholder input as a part of the solar PEIS (BLM 2012b), and these functions are consistent with other studies that have focused on defining the

**Fig. 8** Sensitivity to disturbance index scores mapped to ephemeral stream channels in the vicinity of the De Tilla Gulch SEZ: **a** total index scores, **b** flow and sediment conveyance scores, **c** ecological habitat value scores, and **d** groundwater recharge scores

ecosystem value of ephemeral streams (Nadeau and Rains 2007; Levick et al. 2008; Shaw and Cooper 2008). The landscape characteristics used to stratify the assessment were chosen because other studies have stressed the importance of surficial geology and soil-hydrology conditions with respect to flow and sediment transport (Merritt and Wohl 2003; House 2005; Wohl et al. 2007; Robins et al. 2009), and groundwater recharge (Wilson and Guan 2004; Blasch et al. 2004; Stonestrom et al. 2007). Wildlife habitats in arid regions are closely related to riparian vegetation of ephemeral streams and channel banks (Belnap et al. 2005; Levick et al. 2008; Shaw and Cooper 2008). Watershed-scale datasets on riparian

vegetation communities are scarce, so this study used data on surficial geology and soil-hydrologic conditions to provide habitat information. These surrogate measures of ecological habitat relate to surface water-groundwater interactions that influence vegetation patterns (Sandercock et al.2007).

A slope-based algorithm was developed to identify valley, piedmont, and mountain regions based on similar distributions of slope classes for each analysis watershed (Bowen et al. 2014). For the analysis watersheds in the basin and range physiographic province, the primary differences among the distributions of slope classes were the location and magnitude of the peaks associated with valley regions (Fig. 4a). These

**Fig. 9** Ephemeral streams identified in the highresolution (1:24,000) NHD dataset and 1-m resolution aerial imagery from the National Agricultural Imagery Program (NAIP) within a subwatershed of the Riverside East SEZ

differences loosely correspond with the locations of the analysis watersheds among the five subsections of the basin and range physiographic province, including the Great Basin (the Nevada SEZ watersheds), Mojave-Sonoran Deserts (Riverside East SEZ and the Arizona SEZ watersheds), Salton Trough (Imperial East SEZ watershed), Mexican Highlands (Afton SEZ watershed), and the Sacramento Mountains. The distribution of slope classes for the watersheds in the Southern Rocky Mountains physiographic province of Colorado had a broader (and lower magnitude) peak associated with valley regions, suggesting that more topographic variation is associated with the valley regions (Fig. 4b). A similar pattern among the slope classes of these two physiographic provinces is partially explained by the fact that the Colorado SEZ watersheds were all located in San Luis Valley, which is one of the larger intermontane lowland basins within the Southern Rocky Mountains physiographic province, and these large lowland basins and fault-bounded troughs typically resemble basin valleys of the basin and range physiographic province (Graf 1987).

The peaks in the distribution of slope classes defined mountain and valley regions, but identifying

piedmont regions required a calibration step. Several geomorphic features are found within piedmont regions (e.g., alluvial fans, foothills, and pediments), which coincide with changes in soil and vegetation that allow for multiple interpretations in defining boundaries (Wilson and Guan 2004). The calibration step focused on active alluvial fan features that have distinctive channel patterns and surface color that can be detected visually on aerial imagery (NRC 1996; Alluvial Fan Task Force 2010). Visual inspection of the piedmont regions in the analysis watersheds (e.g., Fig. 2b) suggested that the approach reasonably identified the primary geomorphic features comprising the piedmont regions.

The sensitivity index scores for landscape characteristics were consistent among scorers (i.e., narrow range in scores) except for the hydrologic group variable considering flow and sediment conveyance (index scores ranging between 1 and 4) and the flood frequency variable for ecological habitat (index scores ranging between 2 and 5; Table 4). These variables speak to the frequency of flows in ephemeral streams and the soil conditions controlling runoff and infiltration. From a groundwater recharge perspective, it would be desirable to have more frequent flooding

events over soils that allow for infiltration (hydrologic groups A and B), but more frequent flooding over these types of soils can also result in more erosion and destruction of ecological habitats (Webb and Leake 2006; Archer and Predick 2008). This is an example of where the sensitivity to disturbance is not considered equal among hydrologic and ecologic functions. The sensitivity to disturbance index was generated by averaging the scores of resource specialists. This resulted in there being no instances where a score of 5 (high sensitivity to disturbance) was applied, which limited the sensitivity of the approach. In addition, in instances where resources specialists gave opposite scores, the average resulted in a moderate level of disturbance sensitivity. These artifacts of the scoring methodology somewhat limit the sensitivity of the analysis, but also allow for the examination of stream reaches where the sensitivity to disturbance is not equal for all the ecosystem functions; this can be used to identify locations were targeted mitigation strategies could be implemented.

The sensitivity to disturbance index applied to individual stream reaches in the study watersheds was used to identify highly sensitive reaches that were within SEZ areas and to aid in decisionmaking regarding the defining of nondevelopment areas within SEZs (e.g., Fig. 7). The results presented in the Solar PEIS (BLM 2012b) were for the total index scores because it was assumed that there was a desire to equally maintain the functionalities of flow and sediment conveyance, ecological habitats, and groundwater recharge. There were instances where the index scores for individual stream functions were not fully represented by the total index score; this is similar to the previous discussion about resource specialists having varying opinions with respect to individual components of the sensitivity to disturbance index. An example where the total index score did not reflect all the ecosystem functions can be seen for groundwater recharge at the De Tilla Gulch SEZ (Fig. 8). In this instance, the base of the San Juan Mountains is just to the north of the confining clay layers that cover the majority of the San Luis Valley, and this region serves as the primary location for mountain-front recharge to infiltrate to the lower confined aquifer of the northern San Luis Valley (Mayo et al. 2007). The solar PEIS specified an SEZspecific design feature stating alterations to ephemeral

stream channels and stormwater management plans should emphasize the need to maintain groundwater recharge in the region of the De Tilla Gulch SEZ (BLM 2012b).

The analysis of the Solar PEIS used the total index scores to assign categories of high, moderate, and low sensitivity to disturbance based on the mean and standard deviation of the distribution of index scores over all the analysis watersheds, resulting in a high sensitivity being defined as reaches with total index scores of 60 or greater, moderate sensitivity total index scores between 50 and 59, and low sensitivity total index scores of 49 or less (BLM 2012b). This categorization was done to simplify the results so they could be assessed along with several other metrics for examining overall environmental impacts; however, it should be noted that the discrete distribution of the total score index (Fig. 5) makes it difficult to set threshold levels because moving one index score value to either side of a threshold value could potentially include or exclude several stream reaches. This study focused on the methodology used to derive the ephemeral stream sensitivity to disturbance index and present the results for the index scores themselves, which essentially represents a data-informed, professional-judgment ranking of the assessed stream reaches. Methods used to categorized the index-based rankings can be altered to meet the decision-making needs of the assessment process.

The professional-judgment approach used in developing the sensitivity index was chosen for this study because the assessment had to consider multiple hydrologic and ecological functions of ephemeral streams, for which no comprehensive datasets or process-based models exist at the watershed scale (Turnbull et al. 2008; Steward et al. 2012). Incorporating metrics from datasets and models on flow and sediment conveyance, ecological habitats, and groundwater recharge would be ideal for this assessment approach, and if the study site of interest has enough data to support such analyses then Table 4 could be replaced by the output from these process-based models. While the lack of process-based analyses supporting the sensitivity index can be considered a weakness, the approach can be adapted to allow for expert or stakeholder input to place a “value” score for individual functions and even to weight individual functions differently (not done for this study) (Linkov et al. 2009). It is challenging to plan for land

disturbances that minimize impacts on the many ecosystem processes facilitated by ephemeral streams especially when disturbances can have unequal effects on individual processes and these effects can vary depending upon where in the watershed they occur (Shaw and Cooper 2008). The professionaljudgment approach allows stakeholders to place a value judgment that integrates these multiple factors that can not all be quantified (or quantified to the same level of detail at the watershed scale).

The primary limitation of this assessment approach is that it is applied to stream reaches that are identified in the high-resolution NHD dataset, and several studies have suggested that in arid and semiarid regions, the NHD dataset can underestimate the number of stream reaches by more than 100 % (Caruso and Haynes 2011; Fritz et al. 2013). Figure 9 shows a portion of the Riverside East SEZ on the Palo Verde Mesa with NHD flow lines and HUC12 watershed boundaries. The 1-m resolution imagery from the US Department of Agriculture’s National Agriculture Imagery Program (NAIP) suggests that several ephemeral channel features were not captured by the NHD flow lines (Fig. 9). Unidentified stream reaches are not considered when making decisions about possible land use changes, and these unidentified reaches are unevenly distributed spatially, so the sensitivity to disturbance results can potentially be spatially-biased, depending upon the accuracy of the NHD flow lines. Methodologies for identifying ephemeral stream channels at a very high resolution are needed to improve disturbance assessment approaches, and to inform basic research on the individual ecosystem processes that ephemeral streams facilitate.

There is currently a debate regarding the connectivity of ephemeral streams to jurisdictional waters that fall under the CWA (Izbicki 2007; Nadeau and Rains 2007; Caruso 2011). While several studies have emphasized the importance of ephemeral streams in arid regions, regulatory protections for ephemeral streams are currently piecemeal to nonexistent. Regardless of the availability of regulatory protections for ephemeral streams, managers need to be able to assess actions that involve land disturbances so they can consider low-impact development options. The assessment approach developed in this study was designed to guide planning

efforts for land disturbances associated with utilityscale solar energy development in the southwestern US, and the results were used to inform decisions that lead to identifying nondevelopment and potential mitigation areas. The assessment approach is amendable for future use so it can incorporate quantitative measures of ephemeral stream functions, new landscape characteristic variables, and potentially stakeholder input to the development of the sensitivity index (Table 4). Further research in identifying ephemeral stream channels at very high resolutions in arid regions will benefit this assessment approach by providing a more complete representation of the stream channel networks that can be assessed for potential impacts to ecologic and hydrologic processes.
